title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
The failure here is a model asserting fabricated information as fact. An AI tool called Irys was used to help prepare legal motions, and it produced seven fake case citations spread across eight court filings, along with non-existent quotes and false legal holdings. This is the hallucination failure mode operating inside a high-stakes professional workflow, specifically the drafting of documents submitted to a court as authoritative representations of the law.

The failure reached the filing stage because no one verified the generated citations against actual legal databases before submission. A routine citation check, which is standard in legal practice without AI, would have caught references to cases that do not exist. Lead counsel acknowledged he was unaware AI had been used at all, which points to a gap in oversight at the supervision level as well as at the drafting level.

What is not established is whether the AI tool itself, the lawyers' conduct, or some combination will be found legally sanctionable, as the trial has not concluded and no court ruling on the conduct has been reported.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, non-existent quotes, and false legal holdings in their court filings. The case involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, a postal service worker who sued State Farm after a 2020 fire in her Carson home left it uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, storm damage occurred, and she claims State Farm delayed approving additional repairs, ultimately leaving her home incomplete. She and her husband have since declared bankruptcy and lost their home to foreclosure, stating their family home is permanently gone.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, which resulted in seven fake case citations across eight filings. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court, accepting responsibility despite claiming he was unaware AI had been used. The incident highlights a growing trend in the legal profession, with 41 percent of law firms using generative AI according to recent surveys. A Paris-based database has documented 1,922 legal hallucination cases worldwide, mostly in the United States. The trial is scheduled for October.
